ہزاروں خواہشیں ایسی کہ ہر خواہش پہ دم نکلے
بہت نکلے مرے ارمان لیکن پھر بھی کم نکلے
roman:
hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī ki har ḳhvāhish pe dam nikle
bahut nikle mire armān lekin phir bhī kam nikle
nuance_note: 'nikle' works three ways: 'dam nikalna' (breath leaving, i.e. dying for each desire), 'armān nikalna' (desires fulfilled) and 'kam nikalna' (turned out too few). The irony that even many fulfilled desires fall short must survive.
label: A
gloss: hazāroñ: thousands; ḳhvāhisheñ: desires; dam nikle: breath leaves (to die, or to gasp in agony/ecstasy); armān: longings/yearnings; nikle: emerged/were fulfilled (specifically when paired with armān); kam: few/insufficient
literal:
Thousands of desires such that for every desire, life departs,
Many of my longings were fulfilled, but still, they were few.
poetic:
Thousands of desires, each enough to steal the breath away,
Many longings were sated, yet far too few to stay.
notes:
- The core of the couplet is a brilliant pun on the verb 'nikalna' (to exit/emerge).
- In the first line, 'dam nikle' is an idiom meaning to die or to be breathless with intensity/pain.
- In the second line, 'armān nikle' is an idiom meaning that a longing was fulfilled (literally, the desire 'came out' into reality).
- Ghalib creates a paradox: the desires are so powerful they are lethal, yet the fulfillment of those desires is insufficient to satisfy the soul.
lost: The sonic symmetry of the word 'nikle' repeating at the end of both lines (the radif) is lost. In Urdu, the repetition emphasizes the irony that the same 'exit' (nikalna) represents both the end of life and the fulfillment of a wish.

gloss: hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ: thousands of desires; aisī: such; har ḳhvāhish: each/every desire; pe: on/at; dam nikle: breath would depart (idiom: one would die); bahut: many; nikle: came out/emerged/were fulfilled; mire armān: my longings/desires; lekin: but; phir bhī: even then/still; kam nikle: came out few/too few.
literal:
Thousands of desires are such that at each desire the breath would depart.
Many of my longings came out, but still they came out few.
poetic:
Thousands of desires, each one worth the dying breath—
Many of my longings came to pass, yet still they were too few.
notes:
- dam nikalnā is an idiom for dying; literally it means 'breath coming out'. The literal keeps the breath image, while the poetic 'worth the dying breath' captures the idiomatic force.
- The verb nikalnā is used twice: first with dam (breath departs/die) and then with armān (longings emerge/are fulfilled). English cannot use one verb for both senses; the literal uses 'came out' for both, while the poetic shifts to 'came to pass' for the second.
- armān means heart's longings or desires, often with a sense of unfulfilled yearning. The second line's paradox—many came out, yet still few—suggests infinite desire: even many fulfilled longings feel insufficient.
- The first line is hyperbolic: thousands of desires, each intense enough that one could die at/for it. It sets up the second line's many/few paradox.
- This couplet does not contain Ghalib's takhallus, so no pen-name handling is needed.
lost: The double duty of nikalnā (breath departing vs desire emerging/being fulfilled), the idiomatic force of dam nikalnā as death, the paradox of bahut/kam with the same verb, and the ghazal's rhyme and rhythm cannot be fully carried into English.

gloss: hazāroñ = thousands; khvāhisheñ = desires, wishes; aisī = such; ki = that; har = every; khvāhish = desire; pe = on; dam = breath, life, moment, sigh; nikle = comes out, is drawn, expires; bahut = many; nikle = have come out; mire = my; armān = sighs, longings, sorrows; lekin = but; phir bhī = even then, still; kam = few, little, insufficient; nikle = have come out.
literal:

Many of my sighs have come out, but even so they are few.

Thousands of wishes, each one a breath that must be drawn;

English cannot fully keep the same verb form doing all this work.

roman:
na thā kuchh to ḳhudā thā kuchh na hotā to ḳhudā hotā
Duboyā mujh ko hone ne na hotā maiñ to kyā hotā
nuance_note: Built on 'honā' (to be). Before anything was, God was; had nothing been, God would be; my being drowned me. Had I not been, what would I have been? Implies merging into God (waḥdat al-wujūd). Keep the repetition of 'being'.
label: A
gloss: na thā kuchh: nothing was / there was nothing; to: then; ḳhudā thā: God was; kuchh na hotā: if nothing were; to ḳhudā hotā: then God would be; Duboyā: drowned/ruined; mujh ko: me; hone ne: by being/existence (honā = to be/exist); na hotā maiñ: if I were not; to kyā hotā: then what would be/have been?
literal:
When nothing was, God was; if nothing were, God would be.
Being drowned me; if I were not, then what would be?
poetic:
When nothing was, God was; if nothing were, God would be.
Being has drowned me; had I not been, what would there be?
notes:
- The first line uses a conditional/correlative structure to assert God's necessary existence independent of all contingent things.
- The repeated forms of honā (thā, hotā, hotā, hone, hotā, hotā) create a dense philosophical wordplay on being, existence, and non-existence.
- Duboyā literally means 'drowned'; I keep the water image in the poetic version because it is vivid, though idiomatically it means 'ruined/undid me.'
- Hone ne personifies being/existence as the agent that drowns the speaker—existence itself is the calamity.
- The final kyā hotā is deliberately ambiguous: it can mean 'what would exist?', 'what would happen?', or 'what would it matter?' I chose 'what would there be?' to keep the existential question open.
- The sher has no pen-name (takhallus) in this couplet, so none is rendered.
lost: English cannot carry the compact repetition and polyptoton of honā (thā/hotā/hone) that makes the paradox of being and non-being feel like a single unfolding argument. The final ambiguity of kyā hotā—between 'what would exist,' 'what would happen,' and 'what would it matter'—also cannot be preserved in one English phrase.

ورنہ ہم بھی آدمی تھے کام کے

ishq ne 'ġhālib' nikammā kar diyā
varna ham bhī aadmī the kaam ke
nuance_note: Contrast of 'nikammā' (useless) with 'aadmī the kaam ke' (a man of use). Self-mocking tone, pen name in the final couplet.
label: A
gloss: ishq: love (passionate/divine); ne: (agentive marker); Ghalib: [the poet's pen name, meaning 'dominant']; nikammā: useless, idle, good-for-nothing; kar diyā: made/rendered; varna: otherwise; ham: I/we; bhī: also; aadmī: man/person; kaam ke: capable, useful, of substance
literal:
Love has made Ghalib useless,
Otherwise, I too was a man of use.
poetic:
Love has rendered Ghalib quite idle,
Else, I too was a man of worth.
notes:
- The Takhallus (pen name): Ghalib uses his own name, which means 'the conqueror' or 'the dominant one,' to create a sharp irony: the man whose name implies mastery has been completely defeated and rendered 'useless' by love.
- The Dichotomy: The couplet hinges on the linguistic opposition between 'nikammā' (socially useless/idle) and 'kaam ke' (capable/productive).
- The Lover's Paradox: In the ghazal tradition, the lover is often viewed by society as a madman or a wastrel. Ghalib adopts this self-deprecating persona, playing with the idea that his preoccupation with the Beloved has stripped him of his worldly competence.
- Humor and Wit: Unlike the heavy, tragic tone of many Sufi poets, Ghalib employs a conversational, almost nonchalant wit (zarafat) to discuss his own spiritual or emotional undoing.
- The Royal 'We': The use of 'ham' (we) is the standard poetic convention for the first-person singular, providing a sense of dignity even while discussing his 'uselessness'.
lost: The English cannot fully capture the specific social sting of 'nikammā,' which implies not just being idle, but being a burden to society. ورنہ ہم بھی آدمی تھے کام کے
roman:
ishq ne 'ġhālib' nikammā kar diyā
varna ham bhī aadmī the kaam ke
nuance_note: Contrast of 'nikammā' (useless) with 'aadmī the kaam ke' (a man of use). Self-mocking tone, pen name in the final couplet.
label: C
gloss: ishq = love; ne = ergative marker; Ghalib = pen name (lit. 'dominant/victor'); nikammā = useless, worthless, good-for-nothing; kar diyā = made/rendered; varna = otherwise, or else; ham bhī = I too (poetic plural); ādmī = man/person; the = were; kām ke = of work, i.e. useful/competent
literal:
Love made Ghalib useless;
otherwise I too was a man of work.
poetic:
Love has rendered Ghalib good-for-nothing—
otherwise I too was a man of use.
notes:
- The pen name 'Ghalib' means 'dominant' or 'victor,' so there is irony in the one named dominant being made useless by love.
- 'Kaam ke aadmi' is an idiom for a useful, capable person; I rendered it as 'man of use/useful man.'
- The register is deliberately colloquial ('nikamma,' 'kaam ke'), giving the couplet a wry, self-deprecating humor.
- The first-person 'hum' is a conventional poetic/royal plural; English uses 'I'.
- In the ghazal tradition, love's ruin of worldly competence can carry Sufi overtones of self-annihilation, though here the tone is more witty than mystical.
lost: The pun on the pen name Ghalib ('dominant/victor') and the colloquial flavor of 'nikamma' versus 'kaam ke aadmi' cannot be fully carried; English also loses the Persian/Urdu ergative construction and the poetic plural 'hum.'

nuance_note: Contrast of 'nikammā' (useless) with 'aadmī the kaam ke' (a man of use). Self-mocking tone, pen name in the final couplet.
label: D
gloss: ishq: love (passionate/divine); nikammā: useless, idle, good-for-nothing; varna: otherwise, else; ādmī kām ke: a man of use, a capable person, someone of substance.
literal:
Love has made Ghalib useless,
Otherwise, I too was a man of use.
poetic:
Love has rendered Ghalib a man of no worth,
Otherwise, I too was a man of substance.
notes:
- Takhallus: Ghalib includes his pen name in the second line, which is the standard convention for the maqta (the closing couplet of a ghazal).
- Ishq: In the Sufi and Persianate tradition, 'ishq' is an all-consuming, transformative force. Here, it is the catalyst that strips the poet of his worldly productivity.
- Nikammā: This is a self-deprecating term. Ghalib uses it ironically to describe his state of being 'ruined' or 'rendered idle' by his obsession with love/poetry.
- Ādmī kām ke: A common idiom meaning a person of capability or social utility. The humor lies in the contrast between his former 'useful' self and his current 'useless' state of poetic obsession.
- Ham: The use of 'ham' (we) is a poetic convention for 'I,' common in Urdu and Persian poetry to convey a sense of dignity or a shared human experience.
lost: The specific musicality of the Urdu meter and the subtle irony of 'nikammā'—which carries a nuance of 'noble idleness'—are difficult to replicate in English.

dil ke ḳhush rakhne ko 'ġhālib' ye ḳhayāl achchhā hai
nuance_note: Sceptical irony: I know the truth about paradise, but it is a nice thought to keep the heart happy. Must not become pious or flatly atheist.
label: A
gloss: We know the reality of paradise but Ghaleb considers this thought good for keeping the heart happy
literal: We are aware of the truth about heaven but 'Ghaleb' deems it fitting to hold such a notion in order to keep the heart contented
poetic: Though we know what's true, let's think of paradise and find peace in our hearts
notes: - The speaker acknowledges that they are aware of the reality of heaven. 'Ghaleb' is Ghalib's pen name. The thought about heaven is considered beneficial for keeping the heart happy

nuance_note: Sceptical irony: I know the truth about paradise, but it is a nice thought to keep the heart happy. Must not become pious or flatly atheist.
label: B
gloss: We know the reality of heaven but Ghalib, this is a good idea for keeping the heart happy
literal: We know the reality of heaven, but Ghalib, it's a great idea to keep the heart happy.
poetic: We know what heaven means, Ghalib, but it's a fine thought to make the heart contented with it.
notes: - The wordplay is in 'jannat kī haqīqat' (reality of heaven) and 'dil ke ḳhush rakhne' (keeping the heart happy). Ghalib, who was a Sufi, uses the word 'jannat' to mean 'spiritual reality', as in 'jannat-i-baqa' ('permanent reality'). In the last line he uses 'dil' for 'heart' and 'khus rakhna' (to keep happy) for 'to make contented with'. The wordplay is very delicate, but it's not lost in English. 'Khus rakhna' means 'to preserve', which doesn't quite convey the sense of 'make contented with' that Ghalib intended. 'Achcha' (good) is a Sufi word for 'fine thought'.

ham ko ma.alūm hai jannat kī haqīqat lekin

nuance_note: Sceptical irony: I know the truth about paradise, but it is a nice thought to keep the heart happy. Must not become pious or flatly atheist.
label: C
gloss: ham ko = to us; maʿlūm hai = we know; jannat = paradise, Heaven; haqīqat = reality, truth (Sufi: the ultimate truth behind appearances); lekin = but; dil = heart; khush rakhne ko = to keep (it) content, at ease; ʿġhalib = Ghalib (pen name); ye khayāl = this idea, this notion, this belief; achchhā hai = is good, is fine
literal:
We know the reality of paradise, but
to keep the heart content, Ghalib, this idea is good.
poetic:
We know the truth of Heaven, yet
to keep the heart at ease, Ghalib, this notion will do.
notes:
- Haqīqat (reality/truth) carries a specific Sufi weight: it is the ultimate, unmediated truth, the highest level of spiritual knowledge. Khyāl (idea/imagination) is the lower rung in the Sufi hierarchy of experience. The couplet thus enacts a deliberate descent from haqīqat to khyāl — the speaker *chooses* the lower, more comforting level.
- The word khayāl is doing double duty: it means both 'idea' (the concept of paradise) and 'imagination' (the act of imagining it). The speaker is aware that what sustains him is not knowledge but a kind of willing imagination.
- The understated 'achchhā hai' (is good) is deliberately flat — not 'beautiful,' not 'wonderful,' just 'good.' This is the tone of pragmatic, world-worn faith: not blind devotion but a conscious, slightly weary decision to believe for the sake of the heart's comfort.
- The couplet is a quiet act of self-awareness: the speaker knows he is choosing comfort over truth, and says so openly. This meta-awareness is a hallmark of Ghalib's later style.
- The pen name ʿġhalib falls mid-line, as is typical, and the word 'Ghalib' (meaning 'the conqueror/victor') creates an ironic counterpoint: the one who 'conquers' here is not conquering doubt but making peace with it.
lost: The Sufi technical distinction between haqīqat and khyāl as graded levels of spiritual experience is not recoverable in English without a footnote. The flat, almost deflating register of 'achchhā hai' resists translation — English tends to push toward either enthusiasm or dismissal, while the Urdu holds a precise middle ground of quiet, pragmatic acceptance. The ghazal's structural music — the radif and qafiya that bind this couplet to the rest of the poem — is entirely absent.

urdu:
نقش فریادی ہے کس کی شوخیٔ تحریر کا
کاغذی ہے پیرہن ہر پیکر تصویر کا
roman:
naqsh fariyādī hai kis kī shoḳhi-e-tahrīr kā
kāġhzī hai pairahan har paikar-e-tasvīr kā
nuance_note: Famously opaque opening of the Diwan. Alludes to the Persian custom of petitioners wearing paper robes before a ruler: every figure in the picture wears paper, complaining against the playful pen of its maker. Needs annotation; a bare literal version is meaningless.
label: A
gloss: naqsh: image, figure, trace, design; fariyādī: complaining, plaintiff, lamenting; kis kī: whose; shoḳhī-e-tahrīr: playfulness/mischief/brilliance of writing or pen; kāġhzī: made of paper; pairahan: garment, robe; har paikar-e-tasvīr: every form/figure of a picture
literal: The image complains of whose playfulness of writing? / Paper is the garment of every figure of the picture.
poetic: A painted figure cries out—against whose playful pen? / Each image wears a paper robe, again and again.
notes:
- naqsh means both a painted/drawn figure and a written character or trace, so the line conflates picture and writing.
- fariyādī is a legal complainant/plaintiff: the image is not merely sad but formally lodging a grievance against the artist's caprice.
- shoḳhī-e-tahrīr means the playful wit or mischief of the pen/script, suggesting both dazzling calligraphic style and arbitrary creative power.
- kāġhzī pairahan is both literal—the only garment of a painted figure is the paper surface—and symbolic—its body/clothing is insubstantial, fragile, paper-thin.
- In a Sufi register, all phenomenal forms are figures in a divine artwork, wearing paper-thin robes, complaining of the painter’s will.
lost: The English cannot fully carry the double sense of naqsh as both image and letter/writing, the legal complaint embedded in fariyādī, or the compressed Persian-Urdu izāfat that makes shoḳhī-e-tahrīr mean both artistic flair and fateful play.

gloss: naqsh (image/sketch/imprint); fariyādī (complainant/plaintiff); shoḳhi (playfulness/mischief/vivacity); tahrīr (writing/inscription/stroke); kāġhzī (made of paper); pairahan (garment/robe); paikar (form/embodiment/figure); tasvīr (picture/painting)
literal:
The image is a complainant against whose playful writing?
The garment of every figure in the picture is made of paper.
poetic:
The sketch cries out: 'Whose playful stroke is this?'
For every form in the painting wears a garment of paper.
notes:
- Shoḳhi-e-tahrīr: This refers to the 'mischievous' or 'vivacious' stroke of the pen or brush. In a Sufi context, it alludes to the capricious or playful nature of the Divine Creator's hand in fashioning the universe.

No face is seen

notes:

You are not the master of Rekhta, O Ghalib,
They say in the next era, there was also a Mir.
poetic:
You are no master of Rekhta, Ghalib, it is true,
For they say in the ages to come, there lived a Mir too.
notes:
- Rekhta refers to the literary language of the time, which was a blend of Persian and local dialects; by using this word, Ghalib situates his mastery within a specific high-culture tradition.
- The mention of 'Mir' is a direct allusion to Mir Taqi Mir, the legendary poet of the previous generation. Ghalib was famously obsessed with Mir's legacy, often seeking to surpass him while acknowledging his supremacy.
- The couplet employs a 'humble-brag' or a paradoxical irony. By claiming he is not the master because a 'Mir' existed, Ghalib is both showing extreme humility and asserting his own place in the lineage of greatness.
- The phrase 'next era' (agle zamāne) suggests that even in the future, the standard of poetry will be measured against Mir, implying that Ghalib's own work is part of that eternal conversation.
lost: The specific cultural weight of the 'Mir vs. Ghalib' rivalry is difficult to convey; in Urdu, the name 'Mir' carries a weight of 'pathos' (soz) that 'Mir' alone cannot fully communicate in English. The emphatic 'tumhīñ' also adds a layer of self-mockery that is slightly softened in translation.

literal:

آدمی کو بھی میسر نہیں انساں ہونا
roman:
bas-ki dushvār hai har kaam kā āsāñ honā
aadmī ko bhī mayassar nahīñ insāñ honā
nuance_note: 'aadmī' (a human being) vs 'insāñ' (a humane person): even a man can't easily be human. English 'man/human' tends to collapse the distinction. 'bas-ki' is archaic for 'so much so'.
label: A
gloss: bas-ki: so much so / it is such that; dushvār: difficult/arduous; āsāñ: easy; aadmī: man/human (biological entity); mayassar: attainable/available/granted; insāñ: human (in the sense of possessing humanity, virtue, or spiritual nobility)
literal:
So difficult it is for every task to be easy,
Even for a man, it is not attainable to be human.
poetic:
So arduous is the art of making every burden light,
That even man finds it hard to reach the height of humanity.
notes:
- The crux of the couplet lies in the distinction between 'aadmī' and 'insāñ'. While both translate to 'human' or 'man' in English, Ghalib uses 'aadmī' to denote the biological species (the physical being) and 'insāñ' to denote the ideal of humanity (the moral, spiritual, and ethical perfection).
- The first line establishes a philosophical paradox: the 'difficulty of ease.' This sets the stage for the second line, suggesting that the most difficult 'task' of all is the transition from being a biological human to a virtuous one.
- The word 'mayassar' implies not just availability, but something granted or made possible, often suggesting a divine or circumstantial allowance.
lost: The linguistic elegance of using two words for 'human' that are synonyms in common parlance but opposites in a philosophical context. English lacks a natural pair of words that distinguish biological humanity from ethical humanity without adding adjectives.

nuance_note: Mystical topics, such eloquence: we'd think you a saint (valī) if you weren't a wine-drinker. Leaves open whether the wine is literal or mystical; should not be resolved.
label: H
gloss: masā'il = questions, problems, delicate issues; tasavvuf = Sufism, the Sufi path; bayān = discourse, eloquence, expression; valī = saint, one who has attained spiritual proximity to God (a technical Sufi term for the highest station); bāda-khvār = wine-drinker (bāda = wine, khvār = one who consumes); jo…hotā = if…you were (conditional, contrary-to-fact)
literal: These are the questions of Sufism, this is your discourse, O Ghalib— / We would have considered you a saint, had you not been a wine-drinker.
poetic: These riddles of the Sufi way, this tongue of yours, O Ghalib— / We'd have called you saint, had you not drunk the wine.
notes:
- The central irony: in Sufi poetry, wine (bāda) is the paramount symbol of divine intoxication and the mark of the true lover of God. The speaker's 'objection'—that Ghalib is a wine-drinker—is actually the highest possible confirmation of his sainthood. The couplet praises by appearing to criticize.
- Valī is a technical Sufi term for one who has reached the highest spiritual station (walāya), not merely a generic 'saint.' The English 'saint' flattens this into a Christian connotation.
- The conditional jo…hotā (if…you were) creates a contrary-to-fact structure: the speaker is saying 'you ARE a wine-drinker, and therefore you ARE a saint' while grammatically framing it as a missed opportunity.
- The pen name Ghalib (meaning 'the Conqueror') sits at the end of the first line in its traditional position as radif, and the word itself carries a quiet irony—the 'conqueror' is conquered by wine.
- Masā'il (plural of mas'ala) suggests not just 'questions' but 'delicate, knotty issues'—the thorny problems of the Sufi path that only a true master can address.
lost: The Sufi double meaning of bāda (literal wine / the wine of divine love) cannot be sustained in English without a gloss; 'wine' in English poetry carries Romantic or secular connotations, not the specific Sufi symbolism of divine intoxication. The technical weight of valī as a station in the Sufi hierarchy (as opposed to the Christian 'saint') is irreducible. The rhythmic and sonic architecture of the Urdu line, and the way the conditional clause lands as a punchline, are lost in any English rendering.

گو ہاتھ کو جنبش نہیں آنکھوں میں تو دم ہے
رہنے دو ابھی ساغر و مینا مرے آگے
roman:
go haath ko jumbish nahīñ āñkhoñ meñ to dam hai
rahne do abhī sāġhar-o-mīnā mire aage
nuance_note: Hands can't move but the eyes still have life: leave the goblet and flask before me. Wine vessels as the poet's last attachment to life.
label: A
gloss: go = though; haath ko = to the hand; jumbish = movement; nahīñ = not; āñkhoñ meñ = in the eyes; to = but/at least; dam = breath/life/spirit, also a moment; hai = is; rahne do = let stay/remain; abhī = still/for now; sāġhar-o-mīnā = wine-cup and flagon/ewer; mire aage = before me, in front of me
literal: Though there is no movement in the hand, there is life in the eyes; / let the wine-cup and flagon remain before me for now.
poetic: Though the hand cannot stir, in the eyes there is still breath; / leave the cup and the wine-flask a while yet in front of me.
notes:
- 'dam' carries both 'breath/life' and 'moment,' so the eyes are still alive and still capable of a little while; English has to choose one sense.
- The contrast between the motionless hand and the living eyes is an ironic image of weakness or age versus remaining desire.
- 'sāġhar-o-mīnā' are conventional wine implements; in the ghazal/Sufi register they can also suggest spiritual longing or divine wine, though the surface scene is literal.
- 'rahne do' is an imperative to a cup-bearer or attendant: do not remove the wine-things, since sight itself still sustains him.
- The emphatic 'to' after 'āñkhoñ meñ' marks the eyes as the one thing still retaining life.
lost: The single word 'dam' as both breath/life and moment cannot be reproduced exactly; the Persianate resonance of 'sāġhar-o-mīnā' and the compressed metrical syntax are also lost.

gloss: go: although/albeit; jumbish: movement/motion; dam: breath/life/spirit; sāġhar: wine cup/goblet; mīnā: wine flask/decanter
literal:
Although the hand has no movement, there is still breath in the eyes
Let the goblet and the flask remain before me
poetic:
Though my hand has lost its motion, my eyes still hold their breath;
Leave the goblet and the flask before me, just as they are.
notes:
- The contrast between 'jumbish' (physical agency/movement) and 'dam' (vitality/breath) highlights the threshold between life and death; the body is failing, but the soul's vision remains.
- The 'eyes' having 'breath' is a poetic conceit suggesting that as long as the poet can behold his beloved or his symbols of ecstasy, he is truly alive.
- 'Sāġhar-o-mīnā' (the goblet and the flask) is a classic synecdoche for the tavern and the state of intoxication, representing the tools of spiritual or romantic ecstasy.
- In the Sufi tradition, the wine and its vessels are symbols of Divine Love; the poet is requesting that his final moments be spent in a state of 'intoxication' (spiritual proximity) rather than the 'sobriety' of death.
- The couplet captures the 'ghazal' ethos of clinging to one's identity and passion even in the face of inevitable physical dissolution.
lost: The specific rhythmic cadence of the Urdu meter (behr) and the subtle, concessive weight of the word 'go' (although), which sets a tone of defiant resignation that is difficult to capture in English without sounding overly formal.

label: G
gloss: گو = say / even if; ہاتھ = hand; جنبش = movement, motion (Persian); آنکھوں = eyes (pl., oblique); دم = breath, life, spirit; رہنے دو = let it be, leave it; ساغر = wine goblet (Persian); مینا = glass drinking vessel; آگے = in front, before
literal:
Say that the hand has no movement, but in the eyes there is breath.
Let the wine goblet and the glass still remain before me.
poetic:
Say the hand has lost its motion — yet the eyes are full of breath.
Let the goblet and the glass remain before me, for now.
notes:
- دم (dam) carries a triple meaning: literal breath, life/vitality, and in Sufi usage the divine breath or spirit. English 'breath' retains the first two but flattens the Sufi layer.
- ساغر و مینا (sāġhar-o-mīnā) is a stock paired phrase in ghazal poetry denoting the entire apparatus of wine-drinking; together they evoke the scene rather than two separate objects.
- The central contrast is between the inert hand (physical incapacity, inaction) and the living eyes (visual/spiritual aliveness). The poet concedes bodily paralysis but asserts that the eyes — the seat of desire and perception — are still alive.
- گو (go) opens the couplet as a concessive: 'even if' or 'grant that.' It frames the first hemistich as a hypothetical the poet is willing to accept, making the second hemistich's demand ('let them remain') all the more pointed.
- A Sufi reading is available: the body (hand) may be dead to action, but the inner vision (eyes) is animated by the breath of the Divine; the wine (sharab) is the intoxication of divine love, and its mere presence before the poet is sufficient sustenance.
lost: The specific cultural resonance of sāġhar and mīnā as a fixed poetic pairing; the Sufi weight of 'dam' as divine breath; the soft phonetic texture of the Urdu (the repeated 'm' in jumbish–dam, the liquid flow of rahne do); and the subtle ambiguity of whether 'go' addresses a listener or functions purely as a concessive particle.

notes:

gloss: aah: sigh/moan of pain; ik umr: a lifetime/an age; asar: effect/impact; jiitā: lives/survives; zulf: tresses/hair; sar: head/end/conclusion
literal:

Who lives until the end of your tresses?
poetic:
A sigh requires a lifetime to take its full toll,
Who survives until your tresses reach their end?
notes:
- The word 'sar' is the central pivot of the couplet. In Urdu, it means both 'head' and 'end/conclusion'. Ghalib plays on this: the lover is lost in the 'head' of the hair (the tresses) and dies before reaching the 'end' of them.

- There is a structural symmetry between the two lines: the first deals with the time required for a sound of pain to kill, and the second deals with the impossibility of surviving the physical beauty of the beloved's hair.
- The phrase 'hote tak' (until it happens/becomes) creates a rhythmic parallelism that emphasizes the duration of the lover's suffering.

الٹی ہو گئیں سب تدبیریں کچھ نہ دوا نے کام کیا
دیکھا اس بیماری دل نے آخر کام تمام کیا
roman:
ulTī ho ga.iiñ sab tadbīreñ kuchh na davā ne kaam kiyā
dekhā is bīmāri-e-dil ne āḳhir kaam tamām kiyā
nuance_note: 'kaam kiyā' (medicine did not work) answered by 'kaam tamām kiyā' (finished me off). The pun on 'kaam' carries the couplet.
label: A
gloss: ulTī = turned upside down, reversed, thwarted | ho ga.iiñ = became, turned out | sab = all | tadbīreñ = plans, schemes, strategies | kuchh na = not at all, nothing | davā ne = the medicine (agent) | kaam kiyā = did any work, was of use | dekhā = showed, revealed, let see | is = this | bīmāri-e-dil = the illness of the heart | āḳhir = at last, in the end | kaam tamām kiyā = completed the work, finished the task
literal:
All plans turned upside down, the medicine did no work at all
This illness of the heart showed, at last, its work completed
poetic:
Every scheme has turned to ruin, no remedy has availed—
this heart's disease at last has shown its work is done.
notes:
- The word 'kaam' (work) appears in both lines: the medicine's 'kaam' failed, the disease's 'kaam' succeeded. This deliberate repetition creates a bitter parallel that is partially lost in English, where I used 'availed' in line one and 'work is done' in line two to avoid awkwardness while preserving the finality.
- 'bīmāri-e-dil' (illness of the heart) is the stock ghazal metaphor for love-sickness. The 'heart' is simultaneously the physical organ and the seat of emotion; the 'disease' is both a medical condition and the torment of unrequited or impossible love.
- 'davā' (medicine) carries a Sufi double meaning: the remedies one tries for love-sickness—reason, distance, time, distraction—all of which fail against the power of love.
- 'kaam tamām kiyā' (completed the work) is a phrase with dark finality in Urdu, implying the disease has killed or destroyed. In English, 'work is done' carries a similar weight (echoing death-bed language), which I exploited deliberately.
- The personification of the disease as an active agent (via the Urdu agent marker 'ne' and the verb 'dekhā'—it *showed* its work) makes the lover passive, at the mercy of an external force. This agency is preserved in the English rendering.
- 'ulTī' literally means 'upside down'—a more vivid, physical image than 'ruin' or 'naught.' The plans didn't just fail; they inverted, backfired, became their own opposite.
lost: The exact repetition of 'kaam' across both lines, which in Urdu creates a tight structural echo (the medicine's work vs. the disease's work). The physical vividness of 'ulTī' (upside down) is softened to 'ruin.' The specific cultural resonance of 'bīmāri-e-dil' as a recognized stock phrase in the ghazal canon—readers of Urdu immediately hear the entire tradition of love-sickness poetry—has no equivalent shorthand in English. The meter and the musicality of the Urdu line, with its internal rhyme and the weight of the final word 'kiyā' landing in both hemistichs, cannot be replicated.

gloss: ḳhudī: Self, ego, inner spirit; buland: elevated, high, sublime; taqdīr: destiny, fate, divine decree; bande: servant, slave, human being; ḳhud: himself (reflexive); razā: will, desire, pleasure, consent

Make the Self so elevated that before every destiny
God Himself asks the servant, "Tell me, what is your will?"
poetic:
Exalt the Self so high that before destiny is spun,
God Himself asks the servant, "Tell me, what is your heart's desire?"
notes:

- Raza (Will/Pleasure): There is a profound inversion here. Usually, a devotee seeks God's 'Raza' (pleasure/will). Iqbal suggests a state of spiritual maturity where God honors the human's 'Raza' (will/desire), implying a partnership in the unfolding of the universe.

literal:

gloss: خوب = well, excellently; پردہ = veil, screen, curtain; چلمن = hookah (water pipe); لگے بیٹھے ہیں = are sitting, engaged/occupied; صاف = clearly, openly, plainly; چھپتے = hide, conceal; سامنے آتے = come forward, appear; بھی نہیں … بھی نہیں = neither … nor
literal:
The veil is well that they are sitting with the hookah
They neither hide openly nor come forward
poetic:
Good is the veil — they sit with the hookah,

notes:
- پرده (parda) operates on at least three levels: the physical screen or curtain, the social institution of purdah (seclusion), and the Sufi veil between the seeker and the Beloved. The English 'veil' retains some of this layering but loses the specific social weight of purdah in 19th-century Delhi.
- چلمن (chilman, hookah) is not merely a prop but a generator of its own veil — the smoke it produces adds a second, transient layer of concealment over the physical curtain. The couplet thus stacks veils: cloth, smoke, and the ambiguous body between them.

- خوب (khūb) at the opening carries a tone of quiet approval or even delight — the poet admires the ambiguity rather than lamenting it. This is a characteristically Dagh Dehlvi move: finding aesthetic pleasure in a state of unresolved visibility.
- The hookah also anchors the couplet in a specific social scene — a private, likely domestic or harem-adjacent space in Delhi, where a person (possibly a woman in purdah, possibly a lover, possibly a Sufi figure) sits in leisure behind a screen. The object grounds the metaphysics in the material.

label: A

literal:
My heart does not settle in this ruined homeland
Whose is it that has been built in this impermanent world?

My heart will not settle in this ruined homeland—
whose heart, then, is built in this impermanent world?
notes:
- Architectural metaphor sustained across both lines: 'lagtā' (to attach, to take hold) and 'banī' (built) frame the heart as something that should find a foundation but cannot. The English 'settle' and 'built' preserve this spatial logic.
- 'UjḌe dayār' (ruined homeland) carries deep personal weight for Zafar: after the 1857 uprising he was deposed and exiled to Rangoon. His 'homeland' was literally destroyed. The English 'ruined homeland' hints at this but cannot carry the full historical grief.

- 'Nā-pā.edār' is a standard Sufi-ghazal compound (nā- = not, pā.edār = lasting) for the transient, perishing world (fānī). It sets up the central tension: the heart seeks permanence but the world offers only impermanence.

gloss: parvāna = moth; sham.a = candle; raat = night; to ho = let there be / be there (conditional-imperative); jaan dene ko = to give one's life; maujūd = present, available; koī baat = some matter, some cause, some reason
literal:
I am a moth, but let there be a candle, let there be a night
To give my life I am present — let there be some matter
poetic:
I am a moth — but let there be a candle, let there be night
I am here to die — let there be some cause
notes:
- Parvāna (moth) is a stock symbol in Urdu ghazal for the lover consumed by the beloved; here the poet identifies himself with it, reducing his entire self to an insect whose nature is self-immolation.
- Sham.a (candle) is the beloved / the flame of desire. The moth-candle pairing is one of the most enduring images in the tradition (going back to Persian poetry).
- Raat (night) is the necessary condition: the candle is lit at night, the moth is active at night. Night also carries connotations of darkness, secrecy, and the hour of longing.
- Jaan dene ko (to give one's life) operates on two levels simultaneously: for a moth it is literal (it dies in the flame), for the poet it is the ultimate act of self-sacrifice for a cause or a person.
- Koī baat (some matter / some cause) is the couplet's pivot and its quiet brilliance. The poet has made self-destruction his identity and is now asking for the bare minimum — any reason at all — to fulfill that nature. The casualness of 'baat' (a matter, a thing) against the gravity of 'jaan dena' (giving one's life) creates a dark, understated humour.
- The triple repetition of 'to ho' (let there be) functions as a litany or prayer — a desperate, almost liturgical demand. The poet is not requesting gently; he is insisting that the universe supply the conditions for his annihilation.
- Magar (but) in the first line creates the crucial pivot: 'I am a moth' is a statement of identity, but the 'but' shifts to the conditions required for that identity to be realised. Being a moth is not enough; the moth needs its candle and its night.
lost: The incantatory, liturgical rhythm of the triple 'to ho' cannot be fully replicated in English without sounding forced. The Sufi undertone — the moth as the soul drawn irresistibly toward the divine flame, where 'giving one's life' becomes annihilation of the ego (fānā) — is only partially recoverable. The casual register of 'baat' against the weight of 'jaan' produces a specific kind of Urdu understatement (tāqat) that English 'cause' or 'reason' does not quite match; English tends to make the word either too formal or too flat. Finally, the dark comedy of a man who has so thoroughly identified with a moth that he now finds himself *waiting* for the conditions of his own death — and is mildly inconvenienced by their absence — is a tone that resists clean translation.

literal:
I, Meer, have come to God's house having become an infidel;
on my forehead is a qashqa, around my waist is a zunnar.
poetic:
Meer has come to God's house, an infidel—
a qashqa crowns my brow, a zunnar girds my waist.
notes:
- Central Sufi paradox: the true lover of God, having transcended religious formalism, appears to the outward eye as an infidel (kafir) yet stands in the most sacred space—God's house. The devotee who has gone beyond the letter of the law is mistaken for its violator.
- Qashqa (قشقہ): a type of cap or headgear associated with non-Muslims, likely Zoroastrian. It marks the head—the seat of thought and belief—as 'other.'
- Zunnar (زنار): a girdle or belt specifically associated with Zoroastrian priests (magi). In Islamic discourse it is a stock symbol of infidelity. Together with the qashqa, the two markers dress the poet's body head-to-waist in the regalia of 'unbelief.'
- The pen name mīr (میرؔ) appears in the first line with the tashkeel (ؔ) marking it as a proper noun. This is an unusual placement—takhallus typically appears in the maqta' (closing couplet)—suggesting either the matla' or a deliberate self-referential declaration: the poet names himself as the infidel who has entered God's house.

lost: The specific cultural charge of qashqa and zunnar as instantly recognizable markers of Zoroastrian 'otherness' to a South Asian reader; the metrical rhythm and the musical interplay of the long and short syllables in the original; the double resonance of kāfir as both a technical theological term and a colloquial slur; and the full-body visual symmetry (head + waist) that in Urdu creates a complete image of a person 'dressed' in infidelity, which English prose equivalents flatten.
